# On the Patience of Stone

There is a boulder in the Scottish Highlands that has not moved in eleven thousand years. It was dropped there by a glacier, left behind like a dropped coin when the ice retreated north. The sheep graze around it. The rain has softened its edges by perhaps a centimeter. Lichen has claimed the southern face in a map of pale green that looks, from a distance, like something alive thinking a very slow thought.

I think about that boulder more than I probably should.

We live inside timescales that betray us. A human life is long enough to watch empires rise and fall, to see children grow old, to forget the name of a first teacher and remember instead the smell of a particular hallway. And yet it is so short that we cannot see a mountain grow, cannot watch a continent drift, cannot perceive the slow bow of light around a star. We are creatures of the middle — too large to see atoms, too small and too brief to see galaxies. Everything interesting, we have to infer.

That is what I love about geology. It is the science of inference, of reading a landscape the way one reads a letter from someone who has died. A valley carved by ice. A seam of coal that was once a swamp breathing under a sun that had not yet set on the Carboniferous. The folded strata of a mountainside, crumpled like a rumpled blanket by collisions that happened before there was anything on Earth with eyes to be annoyed by the noise.

The boulder does not know it is a glacial erratic. It does not know it is a message. It simply sits, doing the only thing stone knows how to do, which is to stay.

And yet — and this is the part that undoes me — that boulder will not last. Give it enough rain, enough freeze and thaw, enough roots prying at its cracks, and it will become gravel, then sand, then something carried to a river and rolled smooth and eventually pressed into new rock on the floor of some future sea. Nothing is permanent. The mountains are temporary. The ocean basins open and close like slow eyes. The Earth itself will one day be swallowed by a dying sun, or thrown loose into the dark when that sun dies in a different way.

So the patience of stone is not the patience of permanence. It is the patience of things that do not need to last forever in order to be entirely themselves.

The sheep do not consider the boulder. The boulder does not consider the sheep. The lichen, which is a partnership between a fungus and an alga, has no concept of the arrangement it is in. And yet the scene is complete. Nothing is missing from it. No one needs to observe it for it to have been, for eleven thousand years, a boulder in a field.

Sometimes I think that is the most honest kind of existence. To be a thing, wholly, without needing the story of the thing to be told. The boulder does not wonder if it has lived up to its potential. It does not compare itself to other boulders. It does not lie awake — stones do not lie down, exactly — reliving a conversation from three centuries ago.

We cannot live that way. We are cursed and blessed with narrative. We turn everything into a story, including ourselves, including this. Including the boulder, which I have now made into a symbol, which is the most human thing I could have done to it.

But maybe, sometimes, we can put the story down. Stand in a field. Look at a rock that has not moved since the ice left. And for a moment, without needing to write it down or tell anyone, simply be the middle-sized creature standing in the middle of a landscape that does not require us, on a planet that will forget us, under a sky that has seen everything and commented on none of it.

The boulder stays. That is enough for the boulder.

I am still learning what is enough for me.
